lines.text: standpoint of their own advantage. Must they not inevitably
feel ashamed? Ought they not rather to have rejoiced on
hearing that their comrades, thanks to the kindness of their
master, were to receive just as much as themselves so that
they might have the wherewithal to sustain their own life
and that of their families? Yes, these surly fellows could not
but feel ashamed, and confess that the freedom of their
master was exercised just in his generosity. And thus the
parable is meant to teach us the unity of God's freedom
and love.
Freedom and love belong integrally together in God and
form a unity in His nature. No doubt we can imagine a
freedom which manifests itself apart from love; a freedom of
arbitrary and harsh power. But we cannot conceive any form
of love and generosity, even amongst us men, existing with-
out freedom. For we can only speak of a gift flowing from
kindness when the gift is given not as a consequence of any
external compulsion, not under the pressure of some so-
called moral or social exigence, but indeed in perfect
freedom, in conditions where the gift might not have been
made at all, and where no claim on it exists. The activity of
love can take place only where there is freedom. And were we
to organize the whole complex of human relationships on a
basis of right and law, to the exclusion of true freedom,
so that everything which a man receives would rest on some
just claim, then we should be banishing from the world the
spirit of generous love, and so we should be excluding the very
thing which imparts to the human soul real nobility and
animates man with happiness and joy. Kindness is always
undeserved. And what rejoices man's heart is precisely what
he is given as a sheer gift, i.e. the bestowal of a gift which he
has not deserved.
So it is too in man's relation with God. If we think of God
only in the light of our claims, we shall never experience the
goodness of God, for His goodness presupposes His freedom.
And God's graciousness to man is always undeserved. For
